subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has had 8 months of progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids, with regurgitation of undigested food and occasional nocturnal coughing. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophageal body tapering to a narrow distal segment described as a bird's beak. Manometry demonstrates uncoordinated peristalsis and an elevated resting lower esophageal sphincter pressure.
question: Which of the following best explains the underlying pathophysiology of this condition?

options.text: Degeneration of ganglion cells in the distal colonic wall
Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells
Degeneration of NO- and VIP-containing inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
Fibrosis and atrophy of esophageal smooth muscle with reduced LES pressure
Dilated submucosal veins in the lower third of the esophagus

explanation_correct: Achalasia is caused by degeneration of the inhibitory neurons containing nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophageal wall. Loss of these neurons means the lower esophageal sphincter cannot relax and peristalsis becomes uncoordinated or absent. The resulting functional obstruction produces the classic bird's beak on barium swallow and an elevated LES resting pressure on manometry. Patients have progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, unlike mechanical obstruction which primarily affects solids.

explanation_incorrect.A: This describes Hirschsprung disease, a congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in the distal colon causing a transition zone and failure to pass meconium, not a primary esophageal motility disorder.
explanation_incorrect.B: Autoimmune parietal cell destruction causes autoimmune (pernicious) gastritis with vitamin B12 deficiency; it does not affect esophageal LES relaxation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis with low LES pressure is the esophageal involvement of scleroderma (CREST), which produces reflux rather than a hypertonic nonrelaxing LES.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dilated submucosal veins in the lower esophagus are varices from portal hypertension; they cause painless hematemesis, not dysphagia with a bird's beak deformity.

educationalObjective: Achalasia results from degeneration of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, causing failure of LES relaxation, uncoordinated peristalsis, and a bird's beak on barium swallow.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 52-year-old man reports that over several months he has had increasing difficulty swallowing. He notes it is equally troublesome with solids and with liquids, and he sometimes regurgitates undigested food hours after eating. He has lost 6 kg.
question: Which feature of his dysphagia most strongly favors achalasia over a mechanical esophageal obstruction?

options.text: Dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset
Dysphagia limited to solid foods
Dysphagia with heartburn relieved by antacids
Painful swallowing with white oral plaques
Hematemesis after episodes of forceful retching

explanation_correct: In achalasia, the functional obstruction from a nonrelaxing LES causes dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the outset. This is the key clinical distinction from a mechanical obstruction (such as a tumor or stricture), where a narrowed lumen initially impedes only solids while liquids still pass. The regurgitation of undigested food reflects stasis in a dilated esophageal body.

explanation_incorrect.B: Dysphagia for solids alone suggests a mechanical narrowing, because liquids can still traverse a partially obstructed lumen; achalasia typically affects both consistencies from the start.
explanation_incorrect.C: Heartburn with acid regurgitation points to GERD from transient LES relaxation, not the nonrelaxing hypertonic LES of achalasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Odynophagia with white plaques suggests Candida esophagitis, an infectious mucosal disease seen with immunosuppression, rather than a motility disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hematemesis after forceful retching is characteristic of a Mallory-Weiss mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction, not achalasia.

educationalObjective: Progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids is the hallmark of achalasia and distinguishes it from mechanical obstruction, which typically first affects solids.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 41-year-old man who recently immigrated from rural South America presents with 1 year of progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids and weight loss. Imaging shows a dilated esophagus with a bird's beak deformity, and manometry reveals an elevated LES resting pressure. Serologic testing for a parasitic infection is positive.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his achalasia?

options.text: Autoimmune antibodies against the H+/K+-ATPase
Chronic gastroesophageal reflux with intestinal metaplasia
Eosinophil-predominant infiltration of the esophageal mucosa
Infection with herpes simplex virus type 1
Trypanosoma cruzi infection (Chagas disease)

explanation_correct: Secondary achalasia can result from Chagas disease, caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi and endemic in rural South America, which destroys the myenteric plexus and produces a picture identical to idiopathic achalasia. Extraesophageal malignancies can also cause secondary achalasia via mass effect or paraneoplastic mechanisms. Primary achalasia is idiopathic. The endemic exposure and positive parasitology in this patient make Chagas disease the correct cause.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anti-parietal cell (H+/K+-ATPase) antibodies cause autoimmune gastritis and pernicious anemia, not secondary achalasia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chronic GERD with intestinal metaplasia is Barrett esophagus, a precursor to adenocarcinoma; it does not destroy the myenteric inhibitory neurons.
explanation_incorrect.C: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an atopic, eosinophil-rich mucosal disease with rings and furrows, not a neurodegenerative cause of achalasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: HSV-1 esophagitis causes punched-out ulcers in immunosuppressed patients and presents with odynophagia, not a nonrelaxing LES.

educationalObjective: Secondary achalasia can be caused by Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) or extraesophageal malignancy; primary achalasia is idiopathic.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 38-year-old woman has manometry-confirmed achalasia with absent peristalsis and a high resting LES pressure. She wishes to avoid open surgery and asks about alternatives that can lower LES pressure and improve swallowing.
question: Which of the following is an accepted treatment for this condition?

options.text: Nitrates and calcium channel blockers
Botulinum toxin injection into the LES
Long-term high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy
Topical antifungal therapy
Iron supplementation alone

explanation_correct: Treatment of achalasia is aimed at reducing LES tone and includes surgical myotomy and endoscopic procedures such as botulinum toxin injection into the LES. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, transiently weakening the sphincter and improving emptying. This offers a less invasive option for patients who wish to avoid surgery, though effects are temporary. Neither approach restores normal peristalsis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Nitrates and calcium channel blockers are used for distal esophageal spasm, which has normal LES pressure, not for achalasia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Proton pump inhibitors treat GERD driven by transient LES relaxation; they do not relax a tonically contracted LES in achalasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Topical antifungals treat Candida esophagitis, an infectious mucosal disease, not a motility disorder.
explanation_incorrect.E: Iron supplementation is used for Plummer-Vinson syndrome (dysphagia, iron deficiency anemia, and webs), not for achalasia.

educationalObjective: Achalasia is treated with surgical myotomy or endoscopic botulinum toxin injection to reduce LES tone; nitrates and CCBs are for distal esophageal spasm.
